attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post, stated as his understanding.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'as far as I understand' caveat. That phrase is an epistemic caveat, not a probability or graded-confidence hedge, so the denial stays a scorable observation about ownership.

contract.note: Reading it as conventional legal ownership versus profit-distribution rights is the ordinary reading and matches the surrounding text. The contract expressly accepts an explicit company statement as a source.

evidence.note: Reuters, Dec 8, 2023, inside the target window. It reports Microsoft saying it owns no portion of OpenAI and is only entitled to a share of profit distributions. This is a company disclosure, which the contract accepts.

reviews.rationale: Microsoft's contemporaneous statement, reported by Reuters, says it owns no part of OpenAI and only has a right to share in profit distributions. That meets the support condition. The packet has no counterevidence showing conventional 49% ownership during the period.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A compound observation. The litigation clause stays hedged ('may') and is correctly left unscored. The entitlement, nonprofit-parentage and no-profits parts are preserved.

contract.note: The plain reading of 'profits' as realized net profit since 2019 is fair and ordinary. Correctly, a difference between distribution rights and accounting profit is not treated as a contradiction. The result depends on how the profitability history is read.

evidence.note: Fortune, Jan 2023, citing documents: Microsoft's share drops to 49% until a $92B cap. This supports the capped ~49% entitlement part. Its 2022 loss figure is a projection and only context for profitability.
Law-firm commentary: the nonprofit is the ultimate corporate parent of OpenAI Global LLC. This supports the parentage part only.
Secondary report of a $540M loss in 2022. That is one year with an unspecified basis, so it cannot establish no profits across 2019 to May 2024.

reviews.rationale: The capped ~49% entitlement and nonprofit parentage are supported. The claim that the subsidiary 'hasn't made any profits' is not established: the packet shows only one reported annual loss, with no full history or accounting basis. The contract requires all parts, nothing contradicts any of them, and so the overall claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The rhetorical 'you might think' framing still asserts past conduct. The normalisation captures it fairly.

contract.note: Counting promotion of a military use while OpenAI's policy barred military use as not respecting it is an ordinary reading. It does not require a contractual breach. The result depends on that reading, because Azure OpenAI was reportedly not bound by OpenAI's policies.

evidence.note: The Intercept: Microsoft pitched DALL-E for battle management systems at an Oct 2023 DoD seminar, and Microsoft confirmed the pitch. OpenAI's policy then barred military use, and OpenAI said it was not involved.
WIRED, Mar 2026, before the evaluation date. Both companies say Azure OpenAI was not subject to OpenAI's policies. That rules out a contractual breach, but the stated-preference reading still holds.
OpenAI dropped its blanket military ban in Jan 2024. The Oct 2023 pitch came before that change, so it still falls under the period of OpenAI's stated opposition.

reviews.rationale: Microsoft promoted OpenAI's DALL-E for battlefield systems in Oct 2023, while OpenAI publicly prohibited military and warfare use. That meets the support condition. The Azure terms show there was no binding violation, but the claim concerns respecting a stated wish, not a contract, and nothing shows OpenAI endorsed the pitch.

attribution.note: Marcus states this in his own words while citing The Information, and he endorses it rather than merely quoting it.

semantics.note: Faithful. The project is in-house, large, and positioned against GPT-4, with the Mistral deal as background. The source qualifier is kept.

contract.note: Reading 'big enough to compete' as competitive positioning, not proven parity, is a fair and ordinary reading for an unreleased project.

evidence.note: The Decoder, May 6, 2024, relaying The Information: MAI-1 is an in-house Microsoft model of ~500B parameters, meant to compete with GPT-4 and Gemini. The update says Kevin Scott acknowledged MAI.

Reuters, May 6, 2024: MAI-1 is in-house, not carried over from Inflection, with ~500B parameters. Its use depends on performance, which limits any claim of parity but not the claim that it was being built.
Mistral's Feb 2024 announcement makes Azure its first distribution partner. This establishes the Mistral relationship part. It is a company disclosure, which is adequate for a public partnership.

reviews.rationale: Contemporaneous reporting identifies MAI-1 as an internal Microsoft model of ~500B parameters positioned to compete with GPT-4, and the Mistral partnership is documented separately. Reuters' caveats about performance do not contradict the claim that the model was being built.
